en: The Commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*. Regarding the single character "Bō" (波) [in the title], this sūtra...
[the Buddha] and this Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva both contemplate themselves... even though it is so... [the text continues].

Sentient beings refer to those who uphold, recite, lecture upon, and ultimately practice [this teaching]. When practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, [the term] "Buddha" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), and "pāramitā" refers to reaching the other shore. From the stage of an ordinary person up to the final fruition of sainthood, one uses the power of correct wisdom to destroy delusions and clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty. "Clearly perceiving" means contemplation.
[Blank] aggregates. When a Bodhisattva contemplates these five [aggregates], [they realize they can] cross over all suffering and calamity. "Crossing over" means to transcend.
All suffering [is caused by] sentient beings who, through their persistent delusion, invite these afflictions.
□□□□□□□□□□□□ Śāriputra asked and answered regarding persons whose rank is equal to the Ten Sages.
Because they all share the name "Śāri," it is called "Śā" [Śāri]. Form is not different from emptiness;
emptiness is not different from form. Form is existence; emptiness is non-existence. Form is non-existent... emptiness is non-existent.
Because it is the emptiness external to form, it is said that [form] is not... [form] is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form;
emptiness does not depart from form, and form does not depart from emptiness. Therefore, when viewed through conventional perception, there is existence;
when viewed through wisdom (*prajñā*), there is non-existence. Thus, form and emptiness... [are one].
So too are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Feeling" means experiencing and receiving;
"perception" means conceptualizing and reflecting; "mental formations" mean initiating activity, such as exerting effort and movement.
The cognizer internally conditions what are called the storehouse consciousness, mentation, and so forth.
Since these four dharmas are empty together with form, it is said that "they are likewise so. Śāriputra previously explained provisional emptiness and subsequently clarified the true characteristic.

The Venerable Śāriputra was further commanded: "All dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness; they are neither arising nor ceasing. Even if all dharmas were subject to arising and ceasing, their intrinsic nature is empty and cannot be extinguished. They are neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Because the empty essence of all dharmas is not subject to the shifting and movement of defilement, purity, increase, or decrease, it is said that they are 'not' [so]."
Therefore, within emptiness there is no form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—this further clarifies that the five aggregates are empty.
There is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind—this first clarifies that the six sense bases are empty.
The absence of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects clarifies the emptiness of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
The absence of the eye-element up to the absence of the mind-consciousness-element clarifies the emptiness of the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*).

There is neither ignorance nor the exhaustion of ignorance; the essence of ignorance is illusory and cannot be said to exist, yet it arises simultaneously with the mind and cannot be said to be exhausted.

This extends even to neither old age and death nor the exhaustion of old age and death; sickness, birth, old age, and death manifest from the conditions of karma, being without beginning or end and ultimately unattainable.
There is no conceptual construction of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and nothing to be grasped therein.
There is neither ignorance nor one who attains wisdom; it is with such realization that one gives rise to the bodhicitta.
"Attainment" refers to the characteristics of the fruit of Buddhahood.

When a Bodhisattva approaches the realization of the state of sainthood, both [subject and object] are empty and there is nothing to be attained; because there is nothing to be attained, the Bodhisattva relies upon the Prajñāpāramitā at the time of realizing sainthood.

By means of wisdom, one observes that all phenomena are empty. Because there is no mind to be hooked or obstructed by the movement of attachment or aversion, the mind is without hindrance. Being without hindrance, there is no fear; one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions. A Bodhisattva who possesses the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) has no fear; one who possesses the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) has no dreams or inverted views. This is ultimate nirvana, the final cessation of phenomena, wherein nothing can be apprehended. All Buddhas of the three periods—past, future, and present—rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā. "The three periods" refers to the past, the future, and the present.
Since all realized enlightenment relies upon sublime wisdom, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is translated here as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment."

Because it is without mind, it is like the sun illuminating the distant quarters with vast clarity; thus one knows that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great divine mantra, the great illuminating mantra, the unequaled mantra. When Bodhisattvas realize great Bodhi, they forever sever birth and death.
This reveals the praise of Prajñā through a mind free from doubt:
"The Great Divine Mantra" is the mantra of immeasurable transformations;
"The Great Illuminating Mantra" is the mantra that forever severs the darkness of ignorance.
The unsurpassed mantra is the mantra capable of accomplishing the fruit;

the unequaled mantra is the mantra of the Sole Honored One of the Three Realms, which can eliminate all suffering and is truly not false. When a bodhisattva resolves their mind toward enlightenment, they should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā.
Because it can sever rebirth, remove karmic obstructions, eliminate defilements, and give rise to right faith, it is called the "Dharma-holding Inner Protection," which is true and not false.
Therefore, the Prajñāpāramitā mantra is spoken. The Bodhisattvas praise the Prajñā and exhort its cultivation, and then they speak the mantra, saying:
*Kaṭe kaṭe, parakaṭe, parasamkaṭe, bodhi svāhā.* If a Bodhisattva recites and maintains this mantra,
whether by day or by night.
Wherever this [sūtra] resides, the virtuous deities of the ten directions will constantly come to protect it, so that no demons or malevolent spirits dare to approach.
Therefore, it is called "The Heart Sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom in Which Mantras Are Held for Protection. *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*.
